name: Madurai
info: Madurai is a city on the Vaigai River in Tamil Nadu, India, with a recorded history from the 3rd century BCE, long the capital of the Pandyan kings and later of the Madurai Nayaks.

facts.founded: The city's recorded history is dated to the 3rd century BCE, and the Sangam period settlement site of Keeladi nearby dates to the 6th century BCE.
facts.where: On the banks of the Vaigai River, on a flat and fertile plain south-east of the Western Ghats, in Tamil Nadu, India.
facts.known: The capital of the Pandyas; the Tamil Sangam, said to have been held there; the Meenakshi and Koodal Azhagar temples; the concentric streets laid out under the Nayaks; the sieges of 1763 and 1764; Gandhi's adoption of the loin cloth in 1921; the temple entry movement of 1939
facts.today: Madurai is a major city of Tamil Nadu and the administrative headquarters of Madurai district.

t: Madurai was the capital of the Pandyan dynasty from the 7th century CE, and it passed in turn to the Cholas, the Delhi Sultanate, the Madurai Sultanate, the Vijayanagara Empire, the Madurai Nayaks and the British East India Company in 1801.

The city was built around its temples, and the Nayaks redesigned it as concentric quadrangular streets according to the Shilpa Shastras, a plan that the British kept when they demolished the fortifications in 1837.

Madurai was plundered by Malik Kafur in 1311, fought over in the Carnatic wars and besieged by the English in 1763 and 1764, and in the 20th century it became a centre of the independence and temple entry movements.
dyk: According to the Tamil tradition of the third Sangam, the merit of a poet's work was tested by setting it afloat in the lotus tank of the temple: it was believed that a divine force would make the work of superior merit float and the inferior ones sink.

sections.origins:
Madurai stands on the banks of the Vaigai River, on a flat and fertile plain with an average elevation of 134 metres. The river runs from the north-west to the south-east through the city and divides it into two almost equal halves, and the Sirumalai and Nagamalai hills lie to the north and west. The British archaeologist Robert Bruce Foote found Upper Palaeolithic quartzite tools on the banks of the Vaigai, immediately north of the old town, and sites to the south have been dated to the Mesolithic. Megaliths, dolmens and menhirs of the Neolithic stand at Manamadurai and Perumal Malai, near the city. Iron swords, tools and black and red pottery from the Iron Age show a gradual urbanisation at sites around Madurai.

The recorded history of the city is roughly dated to the 3rd century BCE. The Sangam period settlement site of Keeladi, which dates to the 6th century BCE, lies about 12 kilometres to the south-east. Megasthenes may have visited Madurai in the 3rd century BCE and called it Methora, a view contested by scholars who take Methora to be Mathura in the north. According to Iravatham Mahadevan, a Tamil-Brahmi inscription of the 2nd century BCE calls the city matiray, an Old Tamil word meaning a walled city. Madurai is believed to have been originally a forest of Kadamba trees, which is the origin of the name Kadambavanam.
sections.growth:
The Maturaikkanci, a Sangam work, describes Madurai as the capital of the Pandyas, with fortified gates and towers, a deep moat, a high rampart, two crowded bazaars, broad streets, mansions and markets. It records people of various cultures and languages, artisans and traders who lived in the quarter of their occupation, and markets that stayed active through the night. Greek and Roman writers, among them Strabo, Pliny the Younger and Ptolemy, mention the city, as does the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. Under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I the Pandyan empire reached its greatest extent, from Nellore in the north to Sri Lanka in the south, with Madurai as its capital. Marco Polo, who is considered to have visited India in his reign, wrote that the country was known for its pearls.

Under the Nayaks, who ruled for over 200 years, the city was redesigned and the Thirumalai Nayakkar Palace was built in 1636. The Nayaks financed the spread of agriculture on the black soils, and cotton was grown there in this period on their patronage. The Meenakshi Temple was expanded in several periods, and its present structure was built between 1623 and 1655. Under the British, the Madura Mills, a cotton spinning mill founded in 1889 by the Scots brothers A and F Harvey, turned Madurai into a textile centre.
sections.rulers:
Madurai was the seat of the early Pandyas, and after the Sangam age most of present-day Tamil Nadu, Madurai included, came under the Kalabhra dynasty. The Pandyas under Kadunkon ousted the Kalabhras around 590 CE, and by the 7th century Madurai was the primary capital of the Pandyas, who had also ruled from Korkai until the 5th century. The Cholas took the city in the early 9th century and held it, with the Pandyas ruling as rebellious subordinates, until the early 13th century, when the second Pandyan empire was established with Madurai as its capital.

After the death of Kulasekara Pandian in 1308 his sons fought for the throne, and Malik Kafur reached Madurai in 1311. The city then came under the Delhi Sultanate, and in 1335 its governor Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan declared his independence and founded the Madurai Sultanate. The Vijayanagara Empire, led by Kumara Kampana, ended the sultanate in the 1370s and appointed nayakkanmars as governors. By 1532 the Nayaks were administering Madurai themselves, and they ruled it until 1736, with the capital switching between Madurai and Tiruchirappalli.

Chanda Sahib, sent by the Nawab of Arcot, took Madurai in 1736, and in the Carnatic wars the city changed hands several times. In 1801 the Nawab ceded it to the British East India Company, which annexed it to the Madras Presidency. After independence in 1947 it was part of Madras state and later of Tamil Nadu.
sections.life:
Madurai was built around the Koodal Azhagar and Meenakshi temples, which were the geographic and ritual centre of the ancient city. The Paripatal compares the city to a lotus whose petals are its streets and whose centre is the palace, and the Nayak king Viswanatha (1529 to 1564) redesigned the city as concentric quadrangular streets according to the Shilpa Shastras. The squares keep the names Aadi, Chittirai, Avani-moola and Masi, after Tamil months and their festivals, and the temple chariots grew larger with the size of the street they travelled. The wealthy lived on the streets close to the temple and the poorest on the fringe.

The city was a seat of learning. The three Tamil Sangams, assemblies of Tamil scholars, are said to have been held at Madurai, which is why it was called Koodal, an assembly. Jainism and Buddhism gained prominence in the Kalabhra period, and a Dravida sangam is said to have been founded at Madurai in 470 CE by the Jain monk Vajranandi. Under the Vijayanagara rulers and the Nayaks, large numbers of Telugu, Saurashtra and Kannada people came to the city, and their customs mingled with those of the Muslims and the native Tamils. Mosques such as the Kazimar Big Mosque, said to have been built in the late 13th century, and the Jain centres of Samanar Malai stand beside the Hindu temples. Tamil is the main language of the city, followed by Sourashtra.
sections.crises:
The Pandyan civil war of the 12th century led to a Chola invasion under Kulothunga III, who defeated the Pandyas, destroyed their coronation hall and sowed weeds on its ruins. In 1311 Malik Kafur, hearing of the wealth of the Pandyas and their quarrel over the throne, raided Madurai on 10 April. The Pandyas had fled with their treasures, and Kafur captured the few elephants left at the Meenakshi Temple, plundered it and set it on fire. The Tamil chronicles record that the temple's workers walled up the sanctum and set a second idol before it to save the original, and that the invaders destroyed 14 gopurams. Gangadevi, the wife of Kumara Kampana, wrote that the city under the sultanate had human skulls on iron spikes and Brahmanas beheaded in the streets. Ibn Battuta speaks of an epidemic that killed the population and the fourth Sultan of Madurai, and he condemns the sultan's impaling of Tamil victims.

In the Carnatic wars the English laid siege to Madurai, which was held by Yusuf Khan, in 1763 and were repulsed with heavy losses. In the second siege, in 1764, they surrounded the city on nearly all sides, and in October 1764 they captured it after Captain Marchand, the French commandant, handed Yusuf Khan over to the English and the Nawabs. In 1837 the British demolished the weakened fortifications, drained the moat and built new streets with its debris, and according to the Collector Blackburne the removal of people of the lower castes from the city centre cleared the problem of overpopulation. Many of them were moved to the north-east of the city, which was prone to floods of the Vaigai.
sections.legacy:
The Meenakshi Temple, the Koodal Azhagar Temple and the Thirumalai Nayakkar Mahal are the most prominent monuments of Madurai. The temple, whose complex has 14 gopurams, is a significant symbol for Tamils and has been mentioned in Tamil literature since antiquity. Of the old fort, the west gate, the eastern gateway called Vitta Vasal and two sculptures of the wall, Yanaikkal and Simmakkal, remain. The street plan of the old city, with concentric streets around the temple, was kept when the British laid out the new town.

Madurai was also a place of the independence movement. In 1921 Gandhi first adopted the loin cloth there, after seeing agricultural labourers wearing it. In 1939, under the Temple Entry Authorization and Indemnity Act of the Madras Presidency, the restrictions that prohibited Shanars and Dalits from entering Hindu temples were removed, and the temple entry movement was first led at the Meenakshi Temple by A. Vaidyanatha Iyer. The palace of Rani Mangammal houses the Gandhi Memorial Museum.

Madurai became a municipality in 1866 and a municipal corporation in 1971. It is today the administrative headquarters of Madurai district and has a bench of the Madras High Court. The city had a population of 1,470,755 in 2011, and it is called the cultural capital of Tamil Nadu.

summary: Madurai, on the Vaigai River in Tamil Nadu, has a recorded history from the 3rd century BCE and was the capital of the Pandyas and later of the Madurai Nayaks. It was plundered in 1311, besieged in 1763 and 1764 and ceded to the East India Company in 1801. It is now a major city of Tamil Nadu.
notes: START: the articles give no founding. I used -300 with circa true (recorded history from the 3rd century BCE; Keeladi, 12 km away, is dated to the 6th century BCE).

CONFLICT left out: end of the Madurai Sultanate. The main article says gradual annexation by Vijayanagara until 1378; the history article says overthrown in 1371 by Kumara Kampana and also that it ended in 1378. I wrote only 'in the 1370s'.

CONFLICT left out: Nayak independence. Main article says Madurai became independent from Vijayanagar in 1559; the history article says the Nayaks were administering Madurai themselves by 1532. I wrote 'by 1532' (history article) and no 1559.

CHOLA dates: both articles say the Cholas took Madurai in the early 9th century; the history article's headings say 910-1100 and 'Chola dominance until 1216'; the main article says the city changed hands several times in the 12th century. I wrote 'early 9th century' to 'early 13th century' and left out 1216.
Megasthenes' Methora: contested, as both articles say. Marco Polo 'is considered to have visited' the country in Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan's reign: hedged.

Kafur's raid: history article gives 10 April 1311; the elephants taken 'at the Meenakshi Temple'. The destruction of 14 gopurams is credited to 'the invaders' in the Tamil chronicles (the article does not say which invasion); I placed it with the chronicles' account generally. Gangadevi's and Ibn Battuta's accounts are attributed. Ibn Battuta's 'fourth Sultan' died of the epidemic; I did not name him.
Chola sack (Kulothunga III) is from the history article only, in the Pandyan civil war context, 12th century; the article gives no year.
The population 1,470,755 'in 2011' is the main article's figure for the corporation after expansion (the pre-expansion limits gave 1,017,865). I left out the 'as of' phrasing.
Kazimar Big Mosque: 13th century (main) / late 13th century (history), 'said to have been'. I used 'late 13th century' hedged.
